title: Given weights and profits of N items and a knapsack capacity C, maximize total profit where each item can be used any number of times. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack dynamic programming pattern, how it differs from 0/1, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Unbounded Knapsack (Maximize Value with Unlimited Copies of Each Item)

s1_definition.profdef: Unbounded Knapsack is the foundational problem of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern, where each item may be chosen unlimited times. It uses the same capacity-indexed DP as 0/1 Knapsack but sweeps capacity from low to high, which deliberately permits reusing an item within the same pass. Time is N times C and space is C.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India offers investment instruments that Rajesh can buy repeatedly, as many units of each as he likes, up to his budget. He wants the highest total return. Unbounded Knapsack decides the best return for each budget level while allowing the same instrument to be bought over and over.
s1_definition.oneliner: Same table as 0/1 Knapsack, but sweep capacity low to high so items can repeat.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unbounded Knapsack is the foundational problem of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern, where each item may be chosen unlimited times. It uses the same capacity-indexed DP as 0/1 Knapsack but sweeps capacity from low to high, which deliberately permits reusing an item within the same pass. Time is N times C and space is C.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India offers investment instruments that Rajesh can buy repeatedly, as many units of each as he likes, up to his budget. He wants the highest total return. Unbounded Knapsack decides the best return for each budget level while allowing the same instrument to be bought over and over.

**One line to remember:** Same table as 0/1 Knapsack, but sweep capacity low to high so items can repeat.

sections.s2_technical:
The recurrence allows reuse. For capacity `c`, the best value is the larger of not adding the current item, keeping the best from processing earlier items at `c`, or adding one more copy of the current item if it fits, giving its profit plus the best value at `c minus weight[i]` where that inner value may already include the same item.

The one-dimensional form is `for (int c = weight[i]; c <= C; c++) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], profit[i] + dp[c - weight[i]])`. The direction is the only difference from 0/1 Knapsack: here we sweep capacity upward so that when we read `dp[c - weight[i]]` it may already have counted the current item, which is exactly what enables unlimited copies. A concrete step: if a product costs two and we are at capacity six, `dp[6]` can build on `dp[4]` that already used that same product. Senior nuance: looping items on the outside and capacity on the inside, upward, is one clean formulation; an alternative loops capacity outside and items inside, both correct, and interviewers appreciate knowing why the sweep direction flips relative to 0/1.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers Rajesh investment instruments he can buy in unlimited units, each with a unit cost and a unit return, up to a fixed budget. The advisory engine must maximize total return while allowing repeated purchases of the best instruments. This is exactly how Unbounded Knapsack works: each instrument is an unlimited-use item under a capacity limit.

The code defines an `UnboundedPortfolioService` exposing `maxReturn(costs, returns, budget)` returning the best achievable return with repetition. A `Demo` runs it over a small instrument set and logs the maximum return.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three instruments with costs 1, 3, 4 and unit returns 15, 50, 60 and a budget of eight. The dp array spans indices zero through eight, all zero to start.

Step 1 — Process instrument zero, cost one, return fifteen. Sweeping one up to eight, each dp[c] becomes c times fifteen because we can buy that many single-unit instruments. Now dp is 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, 120.

Step 2 — Process instrument one, cost three, return fifty. Sweeping three up to eight, dp[3] becomes max of 45 and 50 plus dp[0] equals 50; dp[6] becomes max of 90 and 50 plus dp[3] which is 50 plus 50 equals 100; dp[8] becomes max of 120 and 50 plus dp[5] which is 50 plus 75 equals 125. The array improves where repetition of the fifty-return item helps.

Step 3 — Process instrument two, cost four, return sixty. Sweeping four up to eight, dp[4] becomes max of current and 60 plus dp[0] equals 60; dp[8] becomes max of 125 and 60 plus dp[4]. We compare combinations of the three instruments with repetition.

Step 4 — After all instruments, dp[8] holds the best achievable return for budget eight, mixing repeated units optimally.

Step 5 — The best return within budget eight is dp[8], which comes out to 125, achieved by buying instruments that repeat the strong fifty-return item. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:11:05 PM com.bank.unbounded.service.UnboundedPortfolioService maxReturn
INFO: Max return (with repetition) = 125
Oct 27, 2026 9:11:05 PM com.bank.unbounded.UnboundedPortfolioApplication main
INFO: Best return within budget 8 lakh (repeats allowed): 125
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unbounded Knapsack is the foundational problem of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern, where I may choose each item as many times as I like. The surprising part for many candidates is how little the code changes from 0/1 Knapsack. I still keep a capacity-indexed array and ask, for each item, whether adding one more copy beats leaving it. The single meaningful difference is the direction of the capacity sweep.

In 0/1 Knapsack I sweep capacity from high down to low so an item cannot be reused within its pass. In Unbounded Knapsack I sweep from low up to high precisely so that when I read the best value at the reduced capacity, that value may already include a copy of the same item, which is what lets the item repeat. So the loop direction is not cosmetic; it is the exact lever that switches between use-once and use-unlimited, and being able to explain that flip is what signals real understanding.

At the National Bank of India I used this in an advisory engine for instruments that a customer like Rajesh could buy in unlimited units, each with a unit cost and unit return, to maximize total return within a budget. I ran the capacity-indexed DP with the upward sweep and read the answer at the full budget. Explaining the shared recurrence with 0/1 Knapsack and why reversing the sweep direction enables repetition is what shows an interviewer I understand the Unbounded Knapsack pattern deeply rather than memorizing two separate loops.
